toolCalls.name: StructuredOutput

output.brief:
The departures are concentrated in the Kestrel team: 8 of the 11 associates who worked on it resigned, against 1 of 13 others. Kestrel associates also averaged about 2,270 recorded hours, with weekend work on 31% of weekends, versus about 1,940 hours and 6% for other matters, and recorded hours probably understate the real load. The problem is workload on Kestrel, not a firm-wide or market trend. Pay and the billable-target change do not fit the pattern, since the same terms apply to people who did not leave.

The gap I cannot close is supervision. Every Kestrel associate reported to Dorian Faulk, so workload and his supervision are tangled together. My confidence that workload is the main driver is moderate, not final.

Next steps: run the confidential interviews (A1), designed to separate supervision from workload before any money is committed. Do not announce the group-wide retention payment or close the review; that would hide the cause. Record matter and supervisor on every exit going forward (A5). If interviews point to workload, consider a contract review team for Kestrel's review phase; if they point to supervision, consider moving supervision.
output.methodChoice: Kepner-Tregoe problem and decision analysis, with evidence limited to two collected items (X6, X5).
